SEARCH HIGHLIGHTS.

Louise Haigh hints at NHS ban on Palantir

Louise Haigh has suggested that Palantir, the US tech giant, will be blocked from working with the NHS.

Ms Haigh, the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, took a veiled swipe at the firm in her speech to the Labour Party conference with a warning that Britain should not be "in hock" to foreign companies in the field of artificial intelligence.

The Prime Minister is reviewing the Government's overall AI strategy amid mounting pressure from Left-wing MPs to cut ties with Palantir because of its work with the Israeli military and US immigration authorities.

In her address to delegates in Liverpool on Sunday, Ms Haigh said: "We can't stick our heads in the sand or wish away these advancements. We have to grasp it. We have to make sure it's the public who are in control, the public who feel the benefits. Because change is inevitable, but progress is not.

"That is why we will apply the same deliberate approach to how this Government deploys AI, so we can deliver the modern public services that taxpayers deserve, building our sovereign capabilities and backing our own incredible tech sector - refusing to be in hock to foreign giants."

The Telegraph understands this comment was aimed at Palantir, which uses AI to help streamline vast quantities of data, and holds multi-million-pound contracts with the NHS, the Ministry of Defence, the Financial Conduct Authority, and at least six police forces.

Andy Burnham will decide within weeks whether to end Palantir's involvement in the health service following a push from Labour MPs to cut ties with the company because of its work with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Israeli Defense Forces.

Palantir was awarded a contract to develop a federated data platform (FDP) in the NHS in November 2023.

But The Telegraph revealed in July that the Prime Minister was considering exercising a break clause next spring that would allow the health service to sever ties with the company two years into its seven-year contract, which is worth £330m.

Manchester city council last week passed a motion, tabled by the Greens, calling for an end to Palantir's FDP in the NHS. Sheffield, Rotherham and East Hertfordshire councils have also passed motions calling for the break clause for Palantir to be exercised in favour of "NHS-owned or UK-based alternatives to be developed and utilised".

Should he choose to tear up the contract, Mr Burnham would have to inform Palantir of his decision in December, before the contract would auto-renew three months later.
